query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Thermal exposure under service-like oxidizing conditions induces rapid nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds along the grain boundaries of the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, sequestering elements that would otherwise form protective surface oxide films. This transformation results in a measurable loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance compared to the initial metastable solid-solution state.
generation.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state
generation.intervention: Controlled high-temperature thermal exposure using two heating schedules: one that remains just below the intermetallic precipitation threshold and one that exceeds it
generation.conditions: Service-relevant temperatures (300–600 °C) in oxidizing/corrosive atmospheres that simulate realistic operating environments
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitated intermetallic compounds, primarily forming along grain boundaries
generation.mechanism: High-temperature conditions trigger the nucleation and growth of intermetallic phases that deplete or trap beneficial elements (such as Mg) away from contributing to the formation of stable, protective oxide films. This loss of protective film continuity leads to increased susceptibility to both corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples heated above the precipitation threshold will show a significant increase in intermetallic phase content with concurrent deterioration in corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to both the initial state and samples heated below the threshold
generation.baseline: The as-cast metastable solid-solution state with minimal intermetallic compounds and established protective oxide behavior
generation.boundary: Performance and transformations are evaluated under service-relevant thermal conditions (300–600 °C) in oxidizing/corrosive atmospheres
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of intermetallic nucleation and the quantitative impact on corrosion and oxidation resistance remain to be fully delineated

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same Mg-containing HEA in its initial metastable state. Subject one set (Set A) to a heating schedule that remains just below the anticipated precipitation threshold, and another set (Set B) to a schedule that crosses the threshold. Conduct the thermal exposures in an oxidizing atmosphere while simultaneously tracking phase evolution using real-time high-temperature synchrotron diffraction and in-situ electron microscopy, along with concurrent corrosion testing.
measurements: Phase evolution via diffraction peak analysis to quantify intermetallic phase fractions
Electron microscopy to image intermetallic precipitates and assess their distribution
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization to measure corrosion resistance
Surface oxide layer characterization (composition and thickness) via appropriate analytical techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Set B (heated through the precipitation threshold) does not exhibit a significant increase in intermetallic content or if there is no corresponding reduction in corrosion and oxidation resistance compared to Set A and the initial state, then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

In situ thermal observations of materials with the high-temperature XRD provide unique information such as temperature-dependent phase transformations, types of new phase formation, and the start and finish temperatures of competing phases in an alloy system []. In situ HTXRD is instrumental in revealing the real-time of oxide formation as well as the type and temperature at which various kinds of oxide form when metals are exposed to high temperatures in air or in another simulated environment. Our HTXRD analysis provided insight into the thermal stability, phase transitions, and high-temperature oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples, which provides significant guidance in the development of high-performance alloys for demanding applications. The surface and cross-sectional microstructure, elemental distributions, and oxide compositions have been examined to further understand the evolution of the oxides. decision.trend: Starting with 2020 work (PMC7579168) on lightweight Al-Mn-Zn-Mg-Si complex concentrated alloys, researchers found considerable intermetallic formation upon heat treatment, indicating that microstructural evolution plays a key role in mechanical properties and potentially in corrosion/oxidation behavior. By 2024 (PMC11330973), high-pressure synthesis of Al55Mg35Li5Zn5 produced a single-phase alloy with excellent strength-to-weight ratio, emphasizing the importance of processing routes in stabilizing or destabilizing phases. In 2025 (PMC12508472), the community showed that conventional manufacturing can yield nonequilibrium chemical short-range order in metallic systems, highlighting that transformations and precipitations can be trapped or altered under certain kinetic pathways. Despite these insights, the precise mechanism by which metastable Mg-bearing high-entropy or complex concentrated alloys transform—especially under service-like conditions that challenge corrosion and oxidation resistance—remains unclear. The stability of protective phases and the kinetics of intermetallic precipitation are still not fully understood.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved exactly how the metastable Mg-containing solid solution evolves under thermal and corrosive conditions, and whether emergent intermetallic phases degrade or enhance the alloy’s corrosion and oxidation performance over time. The core question centers on the pathway and rate of this transformation—particularly how short-range ordering and multiphase formation might trap or release beneficial elements, and thus either preserve or compromise protective surface films.
decision.lever: Use real-time high-temperature synchrotron diffraction and in-situ electron microscopy to track phase evolution, intermetallic nucleation, and microstructure changes in an environment replicating relevant service temperatures (300–600 °C) and corrosive/oxidizing atmospheres. Compare a controlled set of samples (one exposed to a heating schedule designed to remain just below known precipitation thresholds, another heated through suspected transformation ranges) while simultaneously monitoring corrosion and oxidation across these regimes. If, contrary to the mechanistic hypothesis, the samples expected to precipitate intermetallics do not exhibit reduced corrosion/oxidation resistance (or if no distinct intermetallics form), the hypothesis is falsified.
decision.why: Direct, in-situ observations of phase evolution in service-like conditions provide unambiguous mechanistic evidence regarding how Mg-containing HEA microstructures transform and how those transformations influence corrosion or oxidation. Following the emerging literature trends—where breakdown of metastable phases and formation of new compounds are implicated in property changes—this approach tests the hypothesized link between intermetallic precipitation and altered environmental resistance.
